C. K. Thakur: 
Thank you, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us to discuss the results for the 
second quarter first half of fiscal 2027. As we flagged on our last call, the first half of this year 
turned into a transition period. Our ongoing projects are in their final stages, while 8 new 
projects, 4 in India and 4 overseas were moving through LOA and notice to proceed. 
 
I'll begin with where the industry stands today, because it shapes both our opportunities and our 
discipline. I'll then cover our operating performance and outlook and Ajit, our CFO, will take 
you through the financial updates.  
So, I'll just touch upon the industry overview. India's renewable energy journey continues at an 
extraordinary pace. Renewable and large hydro capacity stood at about 308 gigawatts as of 
September '26, roughly 53% of the country's total generating capacity. 
 
Solar remains the engine of this growth. Installed solar capacity has grown from under 3 
gigawatts in 2014 to about 171 gigawatts today. Calendar 2026 is on track to be the strong year 
for solar capacity addition in India. India added about 34 gigawatts DC in first half of this year, 
38% more than a year earlier and full year additions are expected to be in the range of 50 
gigawatts DC, ahead of the record 49 gigawatts in 2025. 
 
That said, the near term has been more challenging. Two factors slowed new utility scale awards 
in the first half of the year. A third factor, competition, has influenced how we bid.  
First, the shift to domestic solar cells. Since June 2026, projects must use modules made with 
Indian cells as per ALMM-II. India has over 200 gigawatts of module capacity, but about only 
35 gigawatts of cell capacity. So compliant modules are scarce and costly, may raise project 
costs by around 15% to 17%. As a result, developers are reworking project economics and tariffs 
and many have delayed EPC awards until prices and economics settle. We see this as a temporary 
phase. Cell capacity is expected to reach about 100 gigawatts by December 2027, which should 
ease prices and restore award activities. In the long run, it will give India a stronger and more 
secure supply chain.

Second, delay in power purchase agreements and transmission constraints. About 40 to 50 
gigawatts of awarded renewables capacity is still waiting for signed power purchase agreements. 
Solar output is also being curtailed at times in Rajasthan and in some parts of Western India 
because of grid limitations. As a result, projects pipelines in Rajasthan and Gujarat have been 
pushed out of several quarters. 
 
Third, the competitive landscapes. Competitive landscapes has affected how we win the 
projects. Entry barriers in reverse auctions are low and some new players have bid at the prices 
we believe are tough to maintain margins and may not be sustainable. We have been very much 
cautious and selective in such bids and hence, our own order wins in domestic market have been 
lower. We saw similar cycles in 2011 and around 2015-16 and disciplined, experienced players 
came out stronger each time. 
 
The government is now acting firmly on some of the issues related to transmission bottleneck. 
On 30th September 2026, the cabinet approved Green Energy Corridor Phase-III with an 
outlay of around INR1.86 lakh crores. This includes about INR1.36 lakh crores for state 
transmission networks, with central support of around INR54,000 crores. It aims to connect up 
to 135 gigawatts of renewable energy to the grid by financial year 2033. 
 
In addition, on 6 October 2026, the Ministry of Power issued new rules to pay landowners 
market rates for the land used by the transmission lines. This should reduce disputes and speed 
up construction. These measures will take time to deliver, but they directly address the 
transmission bottleneck that is holding back PPAs and new awards. Of course, the blue print of 
this circular has to be seen once the high land cost will come into play. 
 
Battery energy storage systems. Battery storage in India has moved from pilot projects to large-
scale deployment. India added about 8.2 gigawatt hours of battery storage in the first half of 
2026 compared with less than 100 megawatt hours a year earlier. Almost all of this came from 
large stand-alone projects. Rajasthan and Gujarat, two of our core markets account for over half 
of installed capacities.  
The outlook is also robust. CRISIL expects 45 to 50 gigawatt hours to be commissioned in 
financial year 2027 and financial year 2028 alone. Projects with storage made up nearly 40% of 
renewable capacity auction in financial year 2026, up from about 5% earlier. The Central 
Electricity Authority expects 236 gigawatt hours by financial year 2032. The government also 
plans to require storage at new solar and wind projects from July 2027. We expect most large 
solar tenders to include storage going forward.  
We are actively monitoring the BESS opportunities and are selective in bidding new BESS 
projects. Battery prices have risen in 2026 after years of decline. The domestic battery supply 
chain is still developing, and customers increasingly expect long performance warranties from 
EPC contractors.

crores in Q2 and INR3,118 crores in the first half, about 11% lower than H1 FY '26. This decline 
is primarily from our international business. International revenue was INR165 crores in the first

repeat customer. This is our second largest utility scale battery project. We have received the 
LOA. 
 
These wins add to the contract we signed in June 2026 for the West Minya projects in Egypt. 
This is a 1,000-megawatt AC solar plant with 600-megawatt hours of storage worth about USD 
560 million, which will execute through our 50-50 joint ventures with Hassan Allam 
Construction. We expect it to start contributing to revenue this year. Our work under the 5-year 
framework agreement with the Adani Group also continues as planned.

DVC joint venture is nearing completion. Power evacuation will begin once the state 
transmission line is ready. This experience positions us well for upcoming floating solar tenders 
from NTPC- DVC and, DVC alone and several state governments.

27.7 gigawatts last quarter. About 74% of this is in India and 26% overseas. Battery storage bids 
are in addition to this. We see bidding opportunities worth about INR45,000 crores to INR50,000 
crores across solar and storage in the second half of this year.

Now coming to balance sheet and working capital. We continue to operate with negative 
working capital. Net working capital was negative INR301 crores as at 30th September 2026, 
compared with negative INR260 crores at the end of Q1 and negative INR329 crores in March.  
Receivables, including unbilled revenue stood at INR3,005 crores. Receivables days increased 
to 176 from 138 in March and payable days increased to 164 from 135. 
 
Gross borrowings fell by INR244 crores in the first half to INR920 crores as we repaid term 
loans as scheduled. With cash and bank balances of INR319 crores, net debt was INR601 crores, 
broadly unchanged from INR589 crores in March. Shareholders' equity rose to INR719 crores 
from INR651 crores. Most of our existing term loans will be repaid over this year and next year. 
Our banking relationships continue to remain strong. We have secured over INR3,000 crores 
of new credit lines, including local lines in South Africa during the current year, and our lenders 
continue to support as we win orders.

customer once their transaction completes and the balance will be claimed from the promoters

year from the promoters. 
 
To sum up, the first half was a transition period for our international business, while domestic 
EPC and O&M continued to grow. We are well placed for a strong second half with an order 
book of nearly INR12,500 crores, 8 projects moving into execution, a growing O&M business.
